cards.headline: The backing vocal came first
cards.snippet: The backing tracks were cut at the Château d'Hérouville in September 1976, before the song had words. One evening Brian Eno called Mary Hopkin — producer Tony Visconti's wife, visiting with her children — into the studio, and the two of them sang a little 'doo doo' riff in unison, meant as a distant echo. When Bowie heard it, he pushed the fader up until it became one of the record's most prominent sounds. His own vocal, recorded later at Hansa in Berlin, was held back for a full minute and a half — at Eno's insistence, to confound listener expectations.
cards.context: Hopkin was credited as Mary Visconti. She recalled thinking the riff 'very twee' — until Bowie turned it up.

cards.headline: His ultimate retreat song
cards.snippet: Bowie called it his 'ultimate retreat song'. 'It was a very sad song for me,' he said in 2003. 'I was locked in a room in Berlin telling myself I was going to straighten up and not do drugs anymore.' Visconti recalled that more verses existed and were removed at the mixing stage. Released as Low's lead single in February 1977, this hymn to shutting the world out reached No. 3 in the UK — helped by BBC television commercials — while stalling at No. 69 in the US. In 2020 The Guardian's Alexis Petridis named it Bowie's greatest song.
cards.context: The Guardian's verdict came in Alexis Petridis's 2020 ranking of Bowie's songs; Mojo had already placed it fourth in 2015.

cards.headline: The room everyone quotes
cards.snippet: Genius's annotation reads the colour as sadness itself: the single room is isolation and withdrawal, a chainless prison, and the electric blue is the glow of a solitary black-and-white television.
cards.context: One listener painted his whole apartment electric blue thirty years ago, and says he is still holding on to the gift.

lyric.excerptOrTimestamp: Blue, blue, electric blue / That's the colour of my room / Where I will live / Blue, blue
lyric.selectionNote: Quoted by 6 comments across the song's three harvested uploads (top 150 of each; likes 413, 104, 10, 7, 3, 1) — more than any other Genius-annotated line; the next-best line ('Pale blinds drawn all day') reached 2. Full-lyric transcription posts were excluded from the count. The line's Genius annotation scores -19 net votes; selection is by observed quoting frequency.

cards.headline: Nobody lands here by accident
cards.snippet: None of you are here by accident. We all came looking for this song.
cards.context: The 123 replies beneath it are a roll of agreement — nearly every one confirms they came looking on purpose.

replies.author: @geneclark3600
replies.text: yes we did......to pay tribute to The Thin White Duke.

cards.headline: Gifted 1977
cards.snippet: I could have lived in any of the 3 and a half billion years of life on this planet and yet I was gifted 1977 what kind of luck is that
cards.context: His thread fills with listeners comparing birth years; its most-liked reply is the trilobite joke.

replies.author: @robertalexander4588
replies.text: I was 17 myself that year and yeah true words

replies.author: @noe_elaphoros
replies.text: Like you mean you could have been a trilobite instead?

cards.headline: Beyond good and bad
cards.snippet: There is bad music, there is good music, and there is Bowie.
cards.context: The replies argue about labels — the most-liked answers that Bowie transcends 'good' or 'bad' entirely.

replies.author: @paulbudrean571
replies.text: Bowie transcends mere labels such as “good” or “bad”.  He is sui generis.  We are all fortunate to have had him in our lives, unworthy though we may be.

cards.headline: Years ahead, still fresh
cards.snippet: Absolutely years ahead of its time !!!! and yet it feels so fresh!
cards.context: The replies pile on the same verdict in different words — timeless, outside of time itself.

replies.author: @ThePerfidyofPop
replies.text: Because David has been ahead of times in any respect. Fashion, music sounds etc. that makes him so unique! no one can ever replace him...

cards.headline: Beck rebuilds it with an orchestra
cards.snippet: Beck rebuilt the three-minute song as a nine-minute orchestral performance for Lincoln's 'Hello, Again' series in 2013, with an orchestra conducted by his father, David Campbell, plus choir, Alpine horns and a yodeler. One listener: "This is like a 9 minute thesis on why Beck should have done the Bowie tribute at the Grammys."
cards.context: The performance's own thread is full of returning viewers; its most-liked comment calls it a nine-minute thesis.

cards.headline: Live by Request, 2002
cards.snippet: Bowie performed the song for A&E's Live by Request at Sony Music Studios, New York, on 15 June 2002, taking phoned-in requests with a band including Earl Slick, Gail Ann Dorsey and Mike Garson. One listener: "Is not this the most beautiful male voice ever?"
cards.context: Listeners single out the band — Sterling Campbell's drumming and Mike Garson's freewheeling piano draw their own applause.

version.versionLabel: A&E Live by Request, New York (2002)
